entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Thutmose, the revered "King's Favourite and Master of Works, the Sculptor Thutmose," was the preeminent Ancient Egyptian sculptor who flourished around 1350 BCE during the revolutionary Amarna Period. Operating from his expansive workshop in Akhetaten, the new capital founded by Pharaoh Akhenaten, Thutmose was instrumental in defining the distinctive, naturalistic, and often controversial Amarna style that radically departed from traditional Egyptian artistic conventions. His unparalleled skill and direct patronage by Akhenaten positioned him as a central figure in the artistic and ideological transformation of Egypt during the mid-18th Dynasty.

The discovery of Thutmose's ruined house and studio complex in Amarna (modern-day Tell el-Amarna) by Ludwig Borchardt's German archaeological expedition in early December 1912 provided unprecedented insight into an ancient artist's practice. Within this complex, designated P 47.1-3, archaeologists unearthed a treasure trove of sculptures, including numerous portraits of the royal family, unfinished busts, and plaster casts. The most celebrated find, the iconic painted limestone bust of Nefertiti, discovered on December 6, 1912, is widely attributed to his hand and remains a masterpiece of ancient art, showcasing the sophisticated use of color and idealized naturalism characteristic of his work.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Thutmose's workshop and the artifacts discovered within it revolutionized understanding of the Amarna artistic style, providing unparalleled insight into ancient Egyptian sculpting practices and royal iconography. His work, especially the bust of Nefertiti, transcended its original context to become a globally recognized symbol of ancient art.
